title: Knowledge Puffs Up, Love Builds Up
summary: Paul takes up the question of food sacrificed to idols. He agrees with the confident Corinthians that idols are nothing and that there is only one God and one Lord, Jesus Christ. But knowledge without love can destroy a fellow believer, so Paul urges those who feel free to eat to give up that freedom rather than cause a weaker brother or sister to fall.
story: This chapter opens the longest single answer in the letter, running through the end of chapter 10, on how believers should relate to the idol worship that filled their city. Chapter 7 had dealt with marriage; now Paul turns to food and fellowship. He begins not with rules but with the difference between knowledge and love, which will prove to be the key to the rest of the letter: chapter 13 will say that knowledge without love is nothing. Chapter 9 will then give Paul's own example of surrendering rights, and chapter 10 will warn against actual participation in idol worship. Read the three chapters together; this one sets the principle.
historical:
Corinth, like every Greek and Roman city, was full of temples: to Apollo, Aphrodite, Asclepius the healing god, Demeter and Kore, and the cult of the emperor, among others. Excavations at Corinth have uncovered dining rooms at sanctuaries such as the Asclepius complex and the sanctuary of Demeter and Kore, where worshipers and their guests ate meals after sacrifices. Meat from sacrificed animals was eaten at those meals and some was sold in the market. Invitations to such meals came with birthdays, weddings, business associations, and civic festivals.

For wealthier believers, whose social and business lives depended on such networks, refusing to attend temple dinners could mean real loss. Poorer believers rarely ate meat except at public festivals, when it was distributed after sacrifices, so for them meat was closely tied to the gods. Paul had taught the church there was one God, and some members concluded that they could eat anywhere, even in a temple's dining room (verse 10).
cultural:
The ancient world did not separate religion from social life. A banquet in a temple was both a meal with friends and an act done in honor of a god, and a prayer or libation was part of the event. Jewish communities in the Diaspora generally avoided idol-food altogether, a boundary that marked them out from their neighbors. The Corinthians wrote to Paul confident of their own knowledge (verse 1 probably quotes their letter: “We know that we all have knowledge”), and Paul's reply seems to quote other slogans of theirs, such as “an idol is nothing at all in the world” and “there is no God but one” (verse 4).

The “weak” in this chapter are not weak in willpower. They are believers, probably recent converts from paganism, who could not yet eat such meat without feeling they were honoring the god again (verse 7). Conscience in the ancient world meant the inner awareness that judges one's own actions; for Paul, to act against one's conscience, even a mistaken one, damages the person.
literary: Paul first agrees with his readers and then qualifies them, a pattern he uses often in this letter. The opening contrast, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (verse 1), states the theme in a handful of Greek words. Verses 4 to 6 contain a carefully balanced confession: one God, the Father, from whom and for whom; one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom and through whom. Verses 7 to 13 then move from principle to person, ending with Paul's own resolve in the first person: “I will never eat meat again, so that I will not cause him to stumble” (verse 13). That personal turn sets up chapter 9.

doctrines.note: Verse 6 reworks Israel's great confession, the Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4 (the LORD our God, the LORD is one), placing Jesus Christ inside it as the “one Lord” through whom all things came. Paul keeps monotheism and includes Jesus within the identity of the one God, the root of later Trinitarian confession.

Idols are nothing, and there is only one God. Yet Paul does not treat idolatry as harmless; chapter 10 will add that demons stand behind it. Here the danger is that a believer's freedom lures another back into the old worship.

The weak believer is “this weak brother, for whom Christ died” (verse 11). The worth of every member is measured by Christ's death, so to wound a brother's conscience is to sin against Christ himself (verse 12).

words.note: Gnosis, knowledge. The Corinthians prized it, and Paul does not deny its value. But he shows that knowledge alone can inflate a person and injure others; true knowledge begins with being known by God (verse 3). The word would later become the name of the Gnostic movements of the second century, but Paul is not addressing a developed Gnosticism here.

Suneidesis, conscience, the inner faculty that judges one's own actions. Paul says a weak conscience can be “defiled” (verse 7) and “wounded” (verse 12). He does not say the weak are right about idols, but he treats their conscience as something others must protect.

Oikodomeo, to build, build up, or edify. Love “builds up” (verse 1), while knowledge without love tears down. Ironically, in verse 10 Paul uses the same verb to say the weak brother will be “encouraged” (literally built up) to eat, built up into sin. The building metaphor returns throughout chapters 10 and 14.
Proskomma, a stumbling block, something one trips over. In Paul it means something that causes another person to fall into sin or away from faith, not merely something that offends their taste.

christ: Verse 6 is one of the most important statements about Christ in the New Testament. Writing only about twenty years after the crucifixion, Paul places Jesus inside Israel's confession of the one God, as the Lord through whom all things came and through whom we exist. Jesus is the agent of creation and of new creation. The chapter also shows the cross as the measure of how believers treat one another: the weak brother is one “for whom Christ died” (verse 11). Christ gave up everything for that brother; Paul asks the strong to give up a meal. And to sin against a fellow believer is to sin “against Christ” (verse 12), because Christ is one with his people.
questions: Paul says knowledge puffs up but love builds up. When has being right become more important to you than the good of the person you were talking to?
What are the modern equivalents of meat sacrificed to idols, matters where Christians disagree about what is permitted?
Paul was willing to give up meat forever for a brother's sake. What freedom might you give up for someone whose faith is fragile?
